1.title: Ethics, Sustainability and AI
1.text: Welcome to Module 3. This module covers three topics that cut across every domain: ethics, sustainability and artificial intelligence. The last two carry new emphasis in 2026. They rarely appear as stand-alone questions. Instead, they hide inside scenarios about procurement, status reports, planning and risk. In Part 1, we start with the PMI Code of Ethics and how it shapes the best answer.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. Ethics belongs to Business Environment Task 1, which includes ethics and policies. Sustainability appears in four tasks: planning critical information, quality and the cost of quality, compliance requirements and risk execution. AI is new in 2026 and touches all domains. So expect them inside scenarios about planning, quality, risk, procurement and compliance. Know the principles, and learn to recognize them when they are hidden in a story.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Apply the four values and the aspirational and mandatory standards of the PMI Code. Handle conflicts of interest and ethical dilemmas the way PMI expects. Explain sustainability, the pyramid and the triple bottom line, and put sustainability into the project documents. Treat sustainability risks, quality and compliance correctly. Match AI strategies to tasks and describe the main AI terms. And use AI responsibly: validate output, protect data and keep a human accountable.

1.title: Case Check-In: Three Ethics Moments
1.text: Three ethics moments could arise on our microgrid. First, a relative of a team member owns one of the bidders. The best answer is to disclose the relationship and step back from the decision until a mitigation plan is approved. Second, a sponsor wants a late task reported as green. The best answer is to report accurately, with a recovery plan. Third, a supplier offers lavish tickets during bid evaluation. Decline, and follow policy. In all three, law and the Code come before pressure and custom.

1.title: The PMI Code of Ethics
1.text: The PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct describes what we expect of ourselves and of fellow practitioners. It applies to all PMI members, and to non-members who hold a PMI certification such as the PMP, apply for one, or volunteer for PMI. It names four values the global community rated most important: responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty. Each value comes with aspirational standards and mandatory standards. The Code helps practitioners make wise decisions, especially when pressed to compromise integrity or values.

1.title: Aspirational and Mandatory Standards
1.text: Two kinds of standards sit under each value. Aspirational standards describe the conduct we strive to uphold. They are hard to measure, but they are not optional. Mandatory standards are firm requirements. Some limit or prohibit behavior, and violations are subject to disciplinary procedures before PMI's Ethics Review Committee. The Code also carries comments, which give examples and clarification. Comments are not mandatory parts of the Code, but exam questions treat them as expected conduct. One act can breach both aspirational and mandatory standards.

1.title: Responsibility
1.text: Responsibility is the duty to take ownership of decisions, actions and consequences. Aspirationally, act in the interest of society, public safety and the environment. Accept only assignments that match your qualifications. For a stretch assignment, make sure key stakeholders hear about your gaps in good time. Own errors, correct them promptly, and protect confidential information. Mandatory standards: inform yourself of the laws and rules that govern your work, report unethical or illegal conduct, and file complaints only when facts support them. And never retaliate against someone who raises a concern.

1.title: Respect
1.text: Respect is the duty to show high regard for ourselves, others and the resources entrusted to us. Aspirationally, learn the norms and customs of others, and listen to understand. Approach people directly when you disagree, and stay professional even when it is not returned. Avoid gossip. Mandatory standards: negotiate in good faith, and do not use the power of your expertise or position to benefit yourself at others' expense. Do not act abusively, and respect property rights. If an issue is serious or unresolved, go to the proper channel.

1.title: Fairness
1.text: Fairness is the duty to make decisions and act impartially and objectively, free of self-interest, prejudice and favoritism. Aspirationally, be transparent in decisions, and keep re-examining your own impartiality. Give equal access to information to those entitled to it, such as all bidders in a tender. Mandatory standards: proactively disclose real or potential conflicts of interest. Do not hire, fire, reward, punish or award contracts on personal grounds. Do not discriminate. And apply organizational rules without favoritism or prejudice.

1.title: Honesty
1.text: Honesty is the duty to understand the truth and act truthfully. Aspirationally, seek the truth, give accurate information in time, and have the courage to share bad news even when it may be poorly received. Do not bury information or shift blame. Create an environment in which others feel safe to tell the truth. Mandatory standards: do not engage in or condone deception. That includes false statements, half-truths, information out of context, and withholding information in a way that misleads. And no dishonest behavior for personal gain.

1.title: Conflicts of Interest
1.text: Conflicts of interest are one of the most challenging issues in practice. Look for them actively, and help others spot them. When you realize you have one, follow the sequence. Disclose it fully to the appropriate stakeholders. Then step back: do not take part in the decision or try to influence the outcome. Proceed only when you have made full disclosure, have an approved mitigation plan, and have the stakeholders' consent. Treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict. If your brother-in-law's company is bidding, staying silent is not an option.

1.title: Ethics in PMBOK 8
1.text: PMBOK 8 weaves ethics into the whole guide. The accountable leader principle requires integrity, honesty and fairness of everyone. Integrity means sharing risks, stating assumptions and the basis of estimates, delivering bad news early, and making status reports an accurate picture of progress. Respect prefers dialogue, which resolves differences, over debate, which wins or loses. Governance aligns with ethical principles, and ethics and policies sit in process assets. Ethical and reputation risks may not fit numeric scales. Procurement needs impartiality and confidentiality in claims. And AI brings bias, privacy and accountability risks.

1.title: A Practical Flow for Ethical Dilemmas
1.text: Here is a practical flow, labelled as exam practice. Get the facts first. Then put law and the Code ahead of pressure from a boss, a customer or local custom. Act. Disclose conflicts, gaps and errors. Refuse improper requests, such as bribes or falsified status. And report violations to the appropriate body or management, but only on facts. Protect confidential information and the people who raise concerns. And stay direct and professional with the person involved, without gossip. When the options are ignore, do it quietly, or use the right channel, the right channel is usually correct.

1.title: Situations and Best Responses
1.text: Here are five common situations. A vendor offers a lavish gift during bid evaluation: decline and follow policy. A relative's company is bidding: disclose, and step out until a mitigation plan is approved and the stakeholders consent. A sponsor asks you to report green on a late project: report accurately, with the facts and a recovery plan. You find your own estimating or billing error: own it, correct it promptly, and inform those affected. You are asked for a competitor's confidential data: refuse. The theme is truth over comfort.

1.title: More Situations and Best Responses
1.text: Five more situations. You are asked to lead work beyond your experience: disclose your gaps to key stakeholders so they can decide. A local partner demands a facilitation payment: refuse, because it is bribery, take it to legal and compliance, and remember that custom is no excuse. A team member uses unlicensed software: stop it and report to the appropriate management. A colleague reports discriminatory behavior: take it to the appropriate body, protect the reporter from retaliation, and keep it factual. A defect or safety risk would embarrass the sponsor: share it early and factually.

1.title: Ethics in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Ethics is the same in every approach. Only the expression differs. Transparency means accurate status reports, baselines and change logs in predictive work, and information radiators, honest burn charts and open reviews in agile work. Honesty about progress means no watermelon reports, green outside and red inside, and in agile work it means reporting true velocity and impediments, with no inflated story points. Fairness means equal information to bidders, or no favoritism in the backlog. And psychological safety means people can raise issues at gates, or speak up in retrospectives.

1.title: Ethics Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The ethics traps. Truth over comfort: never misreport, and share bad news early, with facts and options. Disclose conflicts, then step back until mitigation is approved. Law and the Code beat custom and pressure, so no bribes, even if they are called facilitation. Report, but on facts, with no unsubstantiated accusations or gossip. Protect confidentiality and intellectual property, and never retaliate. Own your mistakes, and be honest about your qualifications. In procurement and hiring, give equal access to information, with no favoritism or nepotism.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. The Code has four values, with aspirational and mandatory standards, and it applies to certification holders. Responsibility and respect mean ownership, reporting on facts, and direct, professional conduct. Fairness means impartial decisions, equal information and conflicts disclosed. Honesty means truthful, timely information, bad news early, and no half-truths. For a conflict, disclose, step back, mitigate and get consent. For a dilemma, get the facts, put law and the Code first, disclose, refuse or report, and protect people. In Part 2, we turn to sustainability.

2.title: Sustainability: The Principle
2.text: Part 2 covers sustainability, the fifth principle you met in Module 1. The principle says: meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Integrate it across all project areas and all phases. Project managers, teams and sponsors are jointly accountable. It means considering people, planet, society and value in everything you do, at tactical, operational and strategic levels. It belongs to the value-driven side of the mindset, alongside Focus on Value. And it is part of the job, not an add-on.

2.title: The Triple Bottom Line
2.text: The triple bottom line balances three things. Social equity: people. Environmental stewardship: planet. Economic prosperity: profit. Sustainability addresses environmental, social and economic impacts, the well-being of people globally, and the wise use of natural resources. It may include adopting technology responsibly while identifying and mitigating adverse impacts on the organization, community and environment. A project that pays off financially but harms people or the planet is not balanced.

2.title: How Management Orientation Widens
2.text: Management orientation can widen in three steps. Compliance-oriented management focuses on the process life cycle, sponsors and the team. Achievement-oriented management focuses on the deliverable life cycle. Sustainability-oriented management focuses on the outcomes life cycle and on all influential communities, society, stakeholders and posterity. It needs a societal perspective on projects and outcomes, and broad stakeholder engagement, sometimes called management for stakeholders. It also needs responsible leadership, and a holistic focus on the value created and distributed across the wider audience.

2.title: The Sustainability Pyramid
2.text: The sustainability pyramid ranks strategies for any externality a project creates, from most to least desirable. Best: avoid the negative outcome altogether, for example by redesigning so the harm never occurs. Next: minimize the negative outcomes generated. Then: restore the impact of negative outcomes. Least desirable: compensate or offset for the outcomes you generated. So when two options differ, prefer the one higher on the pyramid. Redesign to avoid the harm, rather than offset it afterwards.

2.title: Why Sustainability Matters
2.text: Sustainability brings four kinds of benefit. Organizational: employee satisfaction and retention, better stakeholder relations, resilience, stronger governance and reputation. Operational: innovation in internal processes, and productivity from minimizing waste. Financial: savings from lower material and energy use, lower operating costs and waste, and more investment from sustainable finance investors. Customers and stakeholders: satisfaction, growth in demand for sustainable products and new market opportunities. Sustainability may need additional funding, but it can reduce financial threat to the project and the funding organization.

2.title: Putting Sustainability Into the Project
2.text: How do you put sustainability into the project? Write sustainability key performance indicators into the scope statement, charter, business case, contracts or other authorizing documents. The sponsor confirms them. Then monitor compliance during planning, execution and closure. Doing so needs a societal perspective, broad stakeholder engagement and responsible leadership. Remember that it can add cost and complexity through a broader scope and more stakeholders, and that there are no universal criteria, so success is tailored to the project.

2.title: When Sustainability Goals Are Missing
2.text: What if the business case has no sustainability goals? Suppose the hosting site runs mostly on high-emission power, and the organization has public ESG commitments. Notice the gap. Raise it with the sponsor. Discuss the impact with stakeholders. Seek to confirm goals in the formal documents. Then track the indicators. Do not ignore the gap because it is outside the approved scope, and do not cancel the project or switch suppliers quietly. Even without formal goals, encourage the discussion.

2.title: Sustainability in the Domains: Governance to Finance
2.text: Sustainability appears in every domain. Governance: transparent communication, and sustainability goals built into governance practices. Scope: deliverables meet sustainability goals, and the work breakdown structure or backlog includes activities to manage them, such as assessing carbon dioxide emissions or the impact on local biodiversity. Schedule: minimize carbon footprint and resource use, and let teams offer ideas to accelerate, slow or stop activities. Finance: include sustainability investments that promote long-term savings and environmental benefit.

2.title: Sustainability in the Domains: Stakeholders to Quality
2.text: Now the other domains. Stakeholders: engagement includes sustainability education and collaboration, and some stakeholders hold moral rights, such as protecting a historic site. Resources: prioritize sustainable materials and practices, consider every stage of the value chain, and use green human resource management. Risk: the team sets thresholds, and sustainability helps identify long-term environmental, regulatory and societal risks early. Procurement: source-selection criteria may include sustainability, and contracts can embed environmental, social and governance terms with measurable outcomes. Quality: sustainability is a dimension, and less rework means less waste.

2.title: Sustainability Risks
2.text: Sustainability risks arise when activities fail to balance societal, economic and environmental considerations. Three classic examples. Prioritizing cost over environmental stewardship. Failing to account for community impacts. And underestimating sustainability-related regulatory compliance. The consequences are negative outcomes, stakeholder dissatisfaction, and long-term harm to reputation or performance. Treat them like any other risk: record them in the risk register with owners and responses.

2.title: Sustainability Examples from PMBOK 8
2.text: PMBOK 8 gives examples. In construction, the cheapest materials may harm the environment and health. A sustainability-minded team plans material needs, selects low-impact sources, involves local communities, and considers recycled materials, while still tracking return on investment. In technology projects, eco-friendly practices lower resource use and waste and improve efficiency, and the social impact can include access to education and healthcare. In a renewable energy project, the team tailors risk management with regular stakeholder meetings, regular risk assessments and simulation, to advance green-energy goals.

2.title: Cost of Quality and Compliance
2.text: Two ECO enablers link sustainability to other tasks. For the cost of quality, remember that poor quality and rework consume resources and create emissions and waste. Prevention and appraisal costs are an investment, while failure costs, such as rework, scrap and returns, harm both the budget and the environment. Add sustainability criteria to quality requirements and the definition of done. For compliance, confirm which sustainability requirements apply: environmental regulations, reporting duties and contract clauses. Classify them, check threats to compliance, and monitor throughout.

2.title: KPIs and Tailoring Sustainability
2.text: Here are typical sustainability indicators. These are illustrations. Each project defines its own. Emissions and energy: carbon dioxide equivalent, energy use and water use. Waste and materials: waste diverted from landfill and the share of recycled or sustainable materials. Community: biodiversity and community impact measures. Supply chain: the supplier ESG compliance rate. People: workforce well-being indicators. There are no universal sustainability criteria, so agree the measures with stakeholders. This is exam practice, not PMBOK 8 text.

2.title: Sustainability in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Sustainability looks different by approach. In predictive work, goals live in the charter, business case, scope baseline and contracts, with work breakdown structure activities and budget lines. Compliance is checked at gates and in reports, and risks sit in the register with owners. In agile work, sustainability criteria sit in backlog items and the definition of done. Stories are prioritized by value and re-evaluated each iteration. And risks sit in the risk-adjusted backlog. Hybrid uses a baseline for committed goals and the backlog for evolving ones.

2.title: Sustainability Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The sustainability traps. It is part of the job: include it in scope, risk, quality, procurement and compliance. If goals are missing, raise them with the sponsor. Do not ignore the gap or invent targets. Prefer options higher on the pyramid. Think total value, not the lowest price, and present the trade-off with data. Put it in writing and track the indicators. Tailor the measures, because there are no universal criteria. Accountability is joint among sponsors, project managers and teams. And treat sustainability threats as risks.

2.title: Case Check-In: Sustainability on the Microgrid
2.text: Our microgrid exists to cut campus emissions by about forty percent, so sustainability runs through it. In procurement, supplier sustainability criteria apply to panels and batteries. In scope, the plan includes end-of-life recycling for batteries. In risk, the Eastgate neighbors' concerns about noise, traffic and glare are risks with owners and responses. In quality, less rework means less waste and fewer emissions. Notice that a good business case is not enough: the goals have to show up in the work.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. The principle is to meet present needs without harming future generations, with joint accountability. The triple bottom line balances people, planet and profit. The pyramid says avoid, minimize, restore, then offset. In the project, put the indicators in the documents, have the sponsor confirm them, and monitor throughout. Sustainability shows up in scope work, procurement terms, risks and quality. And when goals are missing, raise them with the sponsor. In Part 3, we cover AI.

3.title: AI in Project Management
3.text: Part 3 covers artificial intelligence, new in the 2026 outline. PMBOK 8 says AI can shift project work from repetitive tasks toward strategy, stakeholder engagement, innovation and improvement. Project managers should be skilled strategists and change managers, with AI supporting decisions, automating routine work and improving forecasting. But the impact of AI depends on the quality of its inputs and on human oversight. So you need to know the terms, the adoption strategies and the risks.

3.title: How the AI Terms Nest
3.text: Four terms nest inside each other. Artificial intelligence is technology that simulates human behavior: systems that can reason, learn and act autonomously. Machine learning is a subfield that uses data to train models that predict outputs. Deep learning is more advanced machine learning, with multilayered neural networks that need large data sets. Generative AI is a subset of deep learning that applies large language models to generate new text, speech, pictures and video. It can draft a charter or summarize a call, but a human must check the output.

3.title: Other AI Tools
3.text: Other AI tools appear in the guide. Natural language processing handles natural language: chatbots, speech recognition, summarization and sentiment analysis. Predictive analytics uses machine learning on current and historical data to forecast performance, trends and risks. Process automation uses rule-based software robots for repeatable tasks, such as scheduling meetings. Genetic algorithms optimize by natural selection, exploring many options, for example in scheduling and resource leveling. Augmented and virtual reality overlay or simulate environments. In every case, a human reviews the output and owns the decision.

3.title: Three Ways to Adopt AI
3.text: PMBOK 8 describes three adoption strategies. Classify tasks by complexity and the need for human supervision. Automation: low-complexity tasks with little human change to the output, such as report generation, document analysis and call summaries, and reusing standard prompts. Assistance: the tool complements your analysis, and first drafts are not complete, like a risk register or a schedule with buffers. A professional reviews for accuracy. Augmentation: complex strategic tasks, where AI is a brainstorming partner, such as balancing a portfolio or forecasting risk.

3.title: AI Use Cases by Domain
3.text: Here are use cases across domains. Governance: data-driven project selection, automated reporting, and early-warning signals from pattern recognition. Risk: identification and assessment from historical data, and impact analysis. Stakeholders: sentiment analysis, used ethically, and personalized communication. Schedule: dynamic scheduling and conflict resolution. Procurement: contract analysis for risk, faster negotiation and compliance. Knowledge: interview bots help capture knowledge, but risk exposing sensitive information and hallucinations. Decide per project where AI assists, and involve the cybersecurity team to judge whether the risk is acceptable.

3.title: Eight Concerns for Responsible Use
3.text: PMBOK 8 names eight concerns for responsible use. Bias: AI trained on biased data or built with biased algorithms. Privacy: AI uses large, sensitive data sets under privacy policies and laws. Accountability: a human must be accountable for each decision. Reliability: check and validate outputs, because they may be biased, incorrect or irrelevant. Safety: design, test and monitor to the required level. Transparency: explain how data is used and how decisions are made. Copyright: ownership of generated content is a dilemma. Sustainability: each request consumes electricity, water and other resources.

3.title: Bias, Privacy and Accountability in Practice
3.text: How do you manage the main concerns? For bias, diversify training data, test periodically with a focus on bias, and involve different teams in development. For privacy, secure the data and collect it under a privacy policy. For accountability, define who is accountable for each decision, and make sure it is a human. For reliability, verify outputs and correct hallucinations before use. Organizational AI guidelines are the foundation for acceptable use. And foster a culture of awareness and ethical use within the team. This aligns with the Code of Ethics: responsibility, honesty and fairness.

3.title: Using AI Well as a Project Manager
3.text: Here is a practical workflow, labelled as exam practice. Decide where AI helps, such as drafting, data analysis and forecasting, and where human judgment must lead, such as stakeholder relationships, ethics and trade-offs. Check policy first: approved tools, data classification, and cybersecurity or legal advice when needed. Protect data: never paste confidential, personal or contractual data into unapproved or public tools. Validate outputs against data and experts. Then decide and document. Treat AI forecasts as inputs, not verdicts.

3.title: AI in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: AI works in every approach. In planning, predictive projects use predictive analytics and baseline optimization, and agile teams use backlog drafting and velocity-based forecasting. In monitoring, predictive projects use automated reports and early-warning signals against baselines, and agile teams use dashboards, burn charts and flow metrics with alerts. In collaboration, AI helps with meeting minutes and reminders, or retrospective summaries and interview bots. The cautions differ: a forecast does not replace baseline governance, and bot summaries do not replace team conversation.

3.title: AI Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The AI traps. A human stays accountable: AI recommends, people decide and own the result. Validate before you trust, because output may contain errors, bias or hallucinations. Protect sensitive data, and use approved tools only. Policy and cybersecurity come first when adopting a new tool. Match the strategy to the task. And when AI conflicts with the team's view, investigate and reconcile. Do not obey it, and do not ignore it. Also be transparent about AI use where it affects people, and know the legal position on generated content.

3.title: Case Check-In: The Dashboard's AI Forecast
3.text: Our dashboard includes a demand forecast that uses AI. Treat the forecast as an input. When it disagrees with the team's view, the team reviews the data and assumptions together, then the product owner and project manager decide. Set guardrails: approved tools only, and no confidential data in public tools. Campus IT security reviews the risk before the tool goes live, and the team documents who decides. That is the pattern the exam rewards: AI informs, humans decide and stay accountable.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Ethics: four values, disclose and step back, truth over comfort, and law and the Code first. Sustainability: avoid before offset, put goals in the documents, and raise gaps with the sponsor. AI terms: artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI. AI strategies: automate, assist, augment. Responsible use: validate, protect data and keep a human accountable. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A project manager discovers that her brother-in-law owns one of the companies bidding on a contract that she helps evaluate. What should she do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Real or apparent conflicts of interest must be disclosed, and the person refrains from the decision until a mitigation plan is approved and the stakeholders consent. Confidence in your own fairness, pressuring the bidder, or reordering the work does not remove the conflict.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. A sponsor under pressure asks the project manager to report the release as on track, although the team is three weeks behind its release plan. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Honesty requires accurate, timely information, and bad news is shared early with facts and options. Shifting the report, reporting green, or giving different versions to different groups all mislead.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. The business case for a data-center migration has no sustainability goals, yet the planned hosting site runs mostly on high-emission power and the organization has public ESG commitments. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Sustainability applies across all project areas, so when goals are missing the project manager still raises the impact with the sponsor and seeks formal confirmation. Proceeding blindly, canceling, or deciding alone skips that discussion.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. A project manager pasted a client's confidential contract terms into a free public AI chatbot to draft a summary. What should she do now? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Confidential data must be protected under privacy and security policy, so she stops, owns the mistake and reports the exposure. Continuing, hiding it, or spreading the practice makes the breach worse.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. An AI forecasting tool predicts that a release will slip by three weeks, but the scrum team believes its sprint plan is sound. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. AI output is an input to be validated, so the project manager reconciles it with the team's analysis and actual progress before deciding. Obeying it, dismissing it, or asking the vendor to change it each skips that validation.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: D. Disclose the conflict and step out until it is resolved. Question two: C. Honesty means reporting the true status with a recovery plan. Question three: A. Raise the missing goals with the sponsor and seek confirmation. Question four: B. Stop, own the mistake and report it under policy. Question five: D. AI output is an input to validate with the team. That completes Module 3. Next, Module 4 covers the common vision, stakeholder engagement and communication. See you there.
